an1.43:1.1: The terminology in this discourse and the next (“corrupted” and “pure”) parallel the verses at [dhp1]()–2. Further connections with these verses are found in the next chapter ([an1.56]()–7. Together, these prose discourses explain the major doctrinal terms of the verses. In fact, it seems likely they belong together as a single discourse; see note on [an1.45:1.1]() below.
an1.43:1.2: Vedic _ābhṛta_ is used for something carried between realms, as the soma is brought from heaven by a hawk (Rig Veda 1.80.2). I understand the phrase _yathābhataṁ nikkhitto_ as a metaphor based on transportation of goods (cf. [dn23:23.52]()).
an1.45:1.1: This simile illustrates the mind after being purified through the practice of absorption ([dn2:98.1]()). | From here through to [an1.55](), the theme shifts from morality to meditation. But this group is split over the formal _vagga_ boundary, leaving each half stranded. It seems likely this was originally a coherent chapter of ten on mental development or meditation, which has become divided during the editorial process. If this chapter were removed, AN 1.44 would lead directly to AN 1.56, and so the two sets of discourses related to [dhp1]()–2 would appear together.
an1.46:1.6: “Unclouded”: free of hindrances due to the practice of absorption (_jhāna_). That absorption is meant is made clear by the reference to “superhuman distinction in knowledge and vision”, which refers to absorptions and the various knowledges that depend on absorption ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj4:4.1.3.1]()).
an1.47:1.1: Varāhamihira says the _phandana_ tree (Sanskrit _spandana_) is good for making cots and seats (_śayyāsana_,  Bṛhatsaṃhitā 79.2), although if the whole cot is _phandana_ it will not conduce to prosperity. His translator N. Chidambaram Iyer identifies it with *Ougeinia oojeinense*, known as the Ujjain desmodium tree or sandan. The sandan’s timber is said to be tough and elastic, and excellent for making furniture. In Pali it is also found at [an3.69:7.4]().
an1.48:1.1: This statement is referred to at [pli-tv-kd3:11.3.4]() by a monk who is afraid he might disrobe due to temptation. Hence, while it is obviously applicable to meditation, it does not directly concern absorption, unlike the rest of this group.
an1.49:1.1: This is perhaps the most misinterpreted passage in the Pali canon. It is not about the metaphysical nature of the mind, but about the mind developed in meditation, as is made clear by the fuller version that starts the next chapter. What is “radiant” is not “the mind” in general; still less is it “naturally” or “inherently” radiant, ideas that contradict everything the Suttas say on the topic. The nature of the mind is not to be radiant, it is to be conditioned. See too note on [an1.21:1.1]().
an1.50:1.2: The “corruptions” from which the mind is freed are the five hindrances ([an5.23:2.4]()). | _Āgantuka_ (“visiting”) elsewhere means “guest”, “visitor”, and its use here is unique. It conveys the sense of something that is not inherent or intrinsic. The point here is that, since corruptions are *not* intrinsic, it is possible to be free from them.
